title: Smooth the icing on a cake's side with a smoother, on a turntable
instruction: Smooth the icing on the side of the cake with the smoother, then put the smoother back in its block.
context: Icing a cake and smoothing its side is a job most people who have baked for a birthday know, and know going wrong: the side stays ridged, the smoother digs in and bares the cake, or a mark is left where the smoother was taken off. Bakers do it with two hands: one holds a straight-edged smoother still and upright against the side while the other turns the cake on a revolving stand, so that the edge cuts the high places down and fills the low ones with the icing it carries; taking the smoother off without a mark is the last skill. Here the cake is a decorator's foam practice round, iced on its side and combed into ridges, on a real revolving stand that turns freely and stands loose on the bench. The score is read on the icing at the end: how even the side is, with no bare place and enough icing left, the cake still centred and the smoother back in its block.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases, x forward, y left. A revolving cake stand (Ateco 612: aluminium top 305 mm across, 3.2 mm thick, 127 mm up, on a cast-iron base, 3.0 kg) stands loose on its non-slip pad at (30, 0); the top turns freely. On it, centred within 0.5 mm on a 1.5 mm mat: a white foam round (152 mm across, 102 mm high, 76 mm radius) on a 203 mm cake board marked with 16 ticks every 22.5 deg. Its side carries 243 g (218 to 268 g) of pale-blue Wilton Creamy White Decorator Icing (medium consistency, 20 to 22 C), turned once under the coarse teeth of an Ateco 1447 held in a jig: ridges 6 mm apart, tops 82.5 +/- 0.5 mm from the axis (6.5 mm icing), valleys 3.0 +/- 0.5 mm deeper, and a 2 mm vertical take-off scar whose place and up to 1 mm out-of-round (inside those 0.5 mm) vary by seed. At (17, -20), a clean Ateco 1447 smoother (aluminium plate 6 x 3.8 in, 152 x 96.5 x 2 mm, 79 g) stands on a short edge in the non-slip 6 x 4 mm channel of a glued beech stand (180 g: base 140 x 80 x 15 mm; 30-deg tilted 140 x 22 x 8 mm cradle, 39 mm rear back, 4 mm front lip, channel floor 27.5 mm up), foot against the lip, leaning on the back, straight 152 mm edge upright along 65 deg from +x. Both arms start at ready; each of the four pads wears a clean powder-free nitrile finger cot. Bench tools: 150 mm steel rule, Vogel 411009 feelers, 3 mm acrylic arc gauge (81 mm radius, 50 mm chord), 24/48/75 mm spacers, depth pin.
scoring: Read at the end of the trial on the side from 9 mm over the board to 9 mm under the top, at 16 ticks on the cake board's rim, every 22.5 degrees, as the README's 'How the side is measured' gives it. Up: a 150 mm steel rule held upright against the side at each tick. Round: a 3 mm acrylic arc gauge (50 mm chord cut concave to radius 81 mm, spanning 36 deg so placements overlap by 13.5 deg) lying level on board spacers 24, 48 and 75 mm high, centred on each tick in turn (48 placements, crossing any mark between ticks). A rule or gauge is laid on lightly, rocked onto each side if it rocks, and lifted straight off; feeler leaves (Vogel 411009) are tried only between its two resting touches where a gap shows. 1.0: the 1.20 mm feeler leaf goes in nowhere under the rule or the gauge; no bare place (white foam on blue icing); mean of 16 depth-pin readings at the ticks at 50 mm height, read last, is 3.0 mm or more; cake within 5 mm of the stand's axis; smoother back in its block; both grippers 3 cm or more from smoother, cake, stand and block. 0.75: the same but for one flaw: every gap over 1.20 mm lies beside one mark at most 2.0 mm high and 21 mm wide, or one bare place under 2 cm2. 0.5: upright-rule gap under 1.50 mm at 8 or more of the 16 ticks; or the side meets 1.0/0.75 while the smoother is out of its block or a gripper is within 3 cm. 0.25: the edge cut at least half the band's height on a quarter of the way round (video). 0: less; cake or stand base 15 mm or more off its place; or over a third of the band bare. Held 1.0 s for early end.
reset_notes: Icing: Wilton Creamy White Decorator Icing, 4 lb (1,814 g) tub, kept closed at 20 to 22 C, stirred, tinted pale blue; one tub ices 7 trials. Between trials (~5.5 minutes): (1) Scrape all worked icing off the foam round and discard it (never reused). (2) Weigh the tub, then spread ~390 g of icing proud all round the 102 mm side with an offset spatula. (3) Place the beech comb jig (V-notched base 250 x 60 x 18 mm against the stand's foot at its bench mark, upright post outside the 305 mm top clamping a second Ateco 1447 with coarse tooth tips set 79.5 mm and notches 82.5 mm from the stand's axis via 3.50 mm feeler leaves), turn the top once slowly by hand, and pull the jig straight radially back to leave the ~2 mm take-off scar. (4) Return the un-worked comb shavings to the tub and re-weigh: net icing on the cake must be 243 +/- 25 g (218 to 268 g). (5) Check four quadrant ticks at 50 mm with the 81 mm arc gauge on ridge tops (gap <= 0.5 mm) and depth pin (6.5 +/- 0.5 mm tops, 3.5 +/- 0.5 mm valley), and verify the board sits within 0.5 mm of the top's centre ring. (6) Stand a washed, dried Ateco 1447 smoother in the wiped, dried beech block at (17, -20), straight edge upright (rotating two smoothers), replace all four powder-free nitrile finger cots, and wipe the turntable and bench clean.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in PhysX. The icing is not a soft body: a 96 x 34 thickness grid on the 102 mm side changed by rules as the smoother's straight edge cuts higher cells onto a blade roll (10 mm2 cap, our estimate), fills cells up to 2 mm below it, leaves remaining roll as a mark on take-off, and hides tiles under 1 mm so white foam shows. Cutting pushes back with 4 kPa (our estimate); gaps are convex-hull depths under the 16 rule and 48 arc-gauge placements. No slumping or sticking.
